name: Ginseng root extract

lead: Ginseng root extract comes from Panax ginseng, a root central to East Asian traditional medicine. In skincare it shows up in K-beauty and herbal products, used for a fresher, healthier, more youthful look.

The chain proponents describe is antioxidant: ginsenosides in the root reduced inflammatory and oxidative signalling in cell and animal studies, which maps to less oxidative stress in skin. Most published research is on oral ginseng for general health, where systematic reviews found efficacy could not be established; no clinical trial of topical use for appearance was found.

paras: Used in creams, essences, serums and herbal soaps as an antioxidant or soothing botanical, usually within a wider anti-aging routine with sunscreen and moisturiser. Some people also take it orally as a supplement. Users describe cumulative, gradual changes over weeks of use.

Oral ginseng has reported side effects, including headache, insomnia and raised blood pressure, and interacts with drugs such as warfarin. Topical products carry standard external-use and irritation warnings.

angle.text: Ginseng root extract is used in K-beauty and herbal skincare as an antioxidant that gives skin a healthier, more youthful look. Ginsenosides lowered oxidative and inflammatory signalling in cell and animal studies, and the research on ginseng is mostly about oral use.

lead: Ginseng root extract is a preparation made from the root of Panax ginseng, a perennial herb native to mountainous parts of Korea, northeast China and the Russian Far East that has long been used in East Asian folk medicine.[1] In skincare it is used as an ingredient in K-beauty and herbal products, where it is marketed mainly as an antioxidant or soothing botanical; one US-listed topical product containing it is a herbal medicated soap.[2] The plant is a slow-growing perennial, 30 to 60 cm tall, and roots are typically harvested at five or six years old; commercial supply comes mainly from China, Korea and Russia, with some production in Japan and Wisconsin.[1]

Most published research concerns oral ginseng and general health outcomes. Systematic reviews of randomised trials found the efficacy of ginseng root extract inconclusive across the indications studied, and laboratory studies have reported anti-inflammatory and antioxidant effects in cells and animals.[3][4][5] Human skin research is limited to small studies such as a Korean trial of an oral red ginseng mixture that measured facial wrinkles and procollagen synthesis.[6]

paras: Panax ginseng has palmately compound leaves with three to five serrated leaflets, a terminal umbel of 30 to 50 flowers, red round fruits and kidney-shaped white seeds. The name is often glossed as man-herb or forked root, referring to the shape of the root.[1] French Jesuit Pierre Jartoux described gin-seng in a letter dated 1711, and said the name refers to the shape of the root.[1] The plant is protected in Russia and China.[1]
Wikipedia identifies ginsenosides as the main phytochemicals under study and describes research on health effects as limited and preliminary, including early work on aging-related disorders.[1]

Ginseng has a long documented place in East Asian medicine. One of the earliest written texts on it as a medicine is the Shennong Ben Cao Jing, dated to 196 AD, and in 1596 Li Shizhen described it as a superior tonic used mainly for chronic illness and convalescence.[7] Control of ginseng fields was contested in China and Korea from the 16th century, and wild ginseng is now described as endangered because harvesting outpaces regrowth.[7]

Roots are sold in several forms. White ginseng is peeled and dried without heating, while red ginseng is peeled, steamed at about 100 degrees Celsius and then dried, giving a reddish, longer-lasting root; red ginseng is the form most often used in Korean extracts and cosmetics.[7] Ginsenosides, a family of steroid saponins, are the signature constituents, alongside polysaccharides, peptidoglycans and polyphenols.[7] Global sales were reported to exceed 2 billion US dollars in 2013, about half from South Korea.[7]

True ginseng belongs to the genus Panax. Wikipedia lists Korean ginseng (P. ginseng), Japanese ginseng (P. japonicus), South China ginseng (P. notoginseng) and American ginseng (P. quinquefolius) among the main species, and notes that unrelated plants such as Siberian ginseng, with a woody root and different compounds called eleutherosides, are also sold under the name.[7]

Fresh ginseng is sold raw (green); white ginseng is peeled and dried without heat; red ginseng is steamed and dried, which makes it less prone to decay.[7] Wild Korean ginseng is described as rare and endangered because it is harvested faster than it regenerates, while cultivated root is cheaper; seeds need a long stratification period and do not germinate until the second spring.[7] In the early 21st century about 99 percent of the world's roughly 80,000 tons came from China, South Korea, Canada and the United States.[7]
Beyond cosmetics, ginseng appears in Korean side dishes, soups, teas and liquor and in energy drinks, herbal teas and supplements.[7]

In cosmetics, ginseng root extract appears in creams, essences and soaps, usually described by brands as antioxidant, revitalising or soothing. A DailyMed-listed topical herbal soap lists Panax ginseng root extract as an ingredient and carries standard external-use warnings: keep out of eyes and stop use if irritation occurs.[2]
Outside cosmetics, ginseng is taken orally for vitality, immune function, cognition, cardiovascular health and sexual function, according to a review of adverse effects.[4]

People who use it on the skin do so for the glow and revitalising feel described in K-beauty marketing, and oral users take it for energy and vitality, which they link to looking rested. The published trials of oral ginseng concern other outcomes.[4]

The appearance chain proposed for ginseng runs through ginsenosides' reported antioxidant and anti-aging activity, to protection against oxidative stress in skin and support for collagen, to fewer visible signs of photoaging. Authors of a Korean trial of an oral red ginseng mixture describe ginsenosides as "believed to have antioxidant, immunostimulatory, and anti-aging activities" and note that no controlled human study had previously examined their effect on photoaged skin.[6] For physique goals, ginseng is also taken in the hope of better stamina and recovery, an application tied to its traditional use among athletes in East Asia.[8]

Ginsenosides and other phytochemicals in the root are the compounds most often studied. A 2022 laboratory and animal study reported that a ginseng root extract reduced inflammatory signalling (MAPK/NF-kB) and activated antioxidant pathways (Nrf2-Keap1) in cultured cells and in a mouse colitis model.[5] These findings come from non-skin models and do not directly test topical appearance effects.

Other laboratory work has examined ginsenoside conversion by microbial enzymes and the use of ginseng extract to synthesise metal nanoparticles; these concern chemistry and materials rather than cosmetic use.

Wikipedia notes that ginseng is generally considered safe for adults for under six months, with possible drug interactions (for example with warfarin) and common side effects including headache, insomnia, raised blood pressure, diarrhoea and skin rash.[1] A systematic review of adverse effects and interactions reached similar conclusions about the oral herb.[4] The product label for the soap advises external use only.[2]

Wikipedia adds that use during pregnancy or breastfeeding is potentially unsafe, that it should not be given to children, and that caution is advised for people with immune disorders, bleeding conditions, cardiovascular disease or cancer; vaginal bleeding is among listed side effects, and long-term use may be unsafe.[1]

Wikipedia also notes that supplement labels do not always match contents, and that the FDA and FTC have sent warning letters over false health claims for ginseng products. It may interact with warfarin, sedatives and several other drugs, and longer use can cause insomnia, headaches and digestive effects.[7]

No clinical studies of ginseng root extract applied topically to the skin for appearance were found. Human trials of oral ginseng exist for other outcomes. A 1999 systematic review of double-blind randomised trials found the evidence for efficacy of ginseng root extract inconclusive across indications.[3] A randomised trial in overweight and obese people with impaired glucose tolerance or diabetes found that ginseng and ginsenoside Re did not improve beta-cell function or insulin sensitivity.[9] Registered trials have examined ginseng extracts for cognition, fatigue, bone metabolism in menopausal women and exercise performance.[10][11]

A randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study in healthy women over 40 tested long-term intake of a red ginseng extract combined with Torilus fructus and Corni fructus. Its title reports that the mixture improved facial wrinkles and increased type I procollagen synthesis in skin; because the product was a multi-ingredient mixture taken orally, the findings relate to that combination.[6]

In a randomised trial of healthy Korean volunteers who took Panax ginseng extract for four weeks, the investigators reported mild adverse events such as dyspepsia, hot flashes, insomnia and constipation in both ginseng and placebo groups, with no serious reactions and no notable changes in blood tests.[12] A small randomised study of eight male college students compared ginseng extract with water around an acute resistance-exercise session, measuring growth hormone, testosterone, cortisol and IGF-1 responses.[8] Wikipedia's review of clinical research reports that confirmed effects on memory, fatigue and menopausal symptoms have not been found in trials.[7]

Wikipedia's ginseng article reports that clinical research has not confirmed effects on memory, fatigue, menopausal symptoms or insulin response in mild diabetes, and that a 2021 Cochrane review found only trivial effects on erectile function.[7]
